data.text: User evaluation is a quick technique that obtains direct feedback from users using self-reports and rating scales. While it is easier than rigorous techniques, identifying suitable questionnaires is a major concern. Collecting data after every task and at the end of a session is desirable if feasible, and questionnaires must be specific to each collection point. Well-known instruments for these purposes include ASQ and EM for tasks, and SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE for sessions.
points: User evaluation is a quick technique that obtains direct feedback from users using self-reports and rating scales.
It is easier than rigorous techniques, but identifying suitable questionnaires is a major concern.
Data can be collected after every task and at the end of a session, which is desirable if feasible, and questionnaires must be specific to each collection point.
Well-known questionnaires include ASQ and EM for tasks, and SUS, CSUQ, QUIS, and USE for sessions.

data.text: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) consists of three statements about task ease, time, and support information, which users rate on a seven-point scale. These statements can be roughly mapped to the ISO usability measures of effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction. Feedback can be summarised by taking the average rating for each statement or for all statements together.
points: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) consists of three statements regarding task ease, time, and support information.
Users rate each statement on a seven-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
The statements can be roughly mapped to the ISO usability measures of effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
Feedback can be summarised by averaging the ratings for each statement or for all statements together.

data.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire with 10 statements that users rate on a 5-point agreement scale. The resulting percentage score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, while lower scores may indicate usability problems. Because SUS provides a quick general indication rather than explaining specific reasons, designers must perform further analysis to identify specific issues.
points: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire with 10 statements given after users complete all tasks.
Users rate each statement on a 5-point agreement scale.
The SUS score is calculated as a percentage, where 70% or higher is typically considered desirable.
SUS gives a quick general indication of usability problems but does not explain the reasons.

data.text: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires, whereas SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ are specifically designed for or relevant to XR cybersickness. Shorter, more precise options like MIS and FMS assess specific conditions, while MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ measure susceptibility to cybersickness. Additionally, the nausea scale and MSAQ are commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive experiences.
points: ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires not specifically meant for XR systems.
SSQ, VRSQ, and CSQ are questionnaires specifically designed for or relevant to XR cybersickness.
MIS and FMS are shorter, more precise questionnaires for assessing specific conditions.
MHQ, MSSQ, and VIMSSQ can be used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness.
The nausea scale and MSAQ are commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive XR.

data.text: The Majuli VR Tour was developed using the Unity engine, XR and VR SDKs, and Autodesk Maya for 3D modeling. Moving videos to cloud services reduced the Oculus Quest application size from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB. The mobile version was optimized to 0.7 GB by compressing images and removing most video support.
points: The Majuli VR Tour was developed using the Unity engine, XR and VR SDKs, and Autodesk Maya for 3D modeling.
Cloud storage reduced the Oculus Quest application size from 9.85 GB to 5.1 GB.
The mobile version reached 0.7 GB by compressing images and removing most video support.

data.text: The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour, a 3D model tour, and a mobile-device tour. The 360-degree-image implementation features a boat-ride experience, a tablet interface with a minimap, and a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method. The 3D model implementation uses 3D models with real-image textures, while the mobile-device tour is a reduced form that omits videos to optimize size.
points: The Majuli VR Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour, a 3D model tour, and a mobile-device tour.
The 360-degree-image implementation features a boat-ride experience, a tablet interface with a minimap, and a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method.
The 3D model implementation uses 3D models with real-image textures to create a realistic appearance.
The mobile-device tour is a reduced form of the full experience that omits many videos to optimize size.
